query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal treatment using solution treatment followed by sub‐recrystallization aging will induce a uniform nano‐precipitate phase in refractory high‐entropy alloys, thereby improving ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys in a cast or cold-rolled state with a coarse microstructure and limited ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply a solution treatment and controlled aging protocol below the recrystallization temperature.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed under sub‐recrystallization temperatures with specific annealing temperatures and aging times to promote a dual-phase microstructure with fine, uniformly dispersed nano‐precipitates. Mechanical testing should be carried out under both quasi‐static and high strain‐rate (impact) loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a fine, uniformly distributed nano‐precipitate phase within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The nano-precipitates activate additional slip systems and delay the onset of damage localization, which increases ductility and uniform deformability while the matrix retains its high strength and ability to release energy upon impact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated samples will exhibit a significant improvement in ductility (e.g., increased fracture strain and uniform deformation) relative to untreated samples while maintaining comparable yield and ultimate strengths and impact-induced energy release capacity.
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloys processed without the controlled thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to refractory high-entropy alloys processed below the recrystallization threshold; results may vary for alloys with substantially different compositions or those undergoing recrystallization.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of ductility improvement and the optimal thermal treatment parameters (annealing temperature and aging time) may vary with alloy composition and require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one set receives the solution treatment and controlled aging (intervention group), and the other is left untreated (control group). Use electron microscopy to quantify nano-precipitate formation and homogeneity. Then, perform mechanical tests under quasi-static and high strain-rate conditions to measure fracture strain, yield strength, ultimate strength, and impact-induced energy release.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution) via electron microscopy
Tensile tests to determine fracture strain and yield strength
High strain-rate (impact) tests to assess ultimate strength and energy release characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ductility (e.g., an improvement of at least ~10% in fracture strain) without a degradation (greater than ~5%) in yield or ultimate strength and impact-induced energy release relative to untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). cited_evidence.text: The quasi-static compressive stress–strain curves of the alloys with varying W contents are presented in Figure 2a. For the W0 alloy, the yield strength (σYS) and the ultimate strength (σUS) are approximately 1620 MPa and 1810 MPa, respectively, with an elongation of ~22%. Serrated steps observed in the stress–strain curve of W0 suggest a susceptibility to plastic instability. The introduction of W into the alloy preserves the high yield strength while significantly improving both fracture strength and fracture strain []. For example, the W13 alloy demonstrates a yield strength of 1650 MPa, along with an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa and a fracture strain of 32%. Figure 2b presents the dynamic engineering stress–strain curves of alloys with varying W contents, tested at high strain rates (2000 s−1) and at room temperature. Under dynamic conditions, the yield strength of each alloy is significantly enhanced compared with the quasi-static conditions. Notably, while the W0 and W8 alloys exhibit poor dynamic plasticity with elongations below 10%, the W13 and W18 alloys demonstrate superior dynamic mechanical properties, achieving ultra-high dynamic yield strengths (exceeding 2200 MPa)

This study demonstrates that the addition of W significantly enhances the mechanical properties of TiZrMo alloys, with the phase ratio effectively being controlled by adjusting the elemental composition. As a result, a dual-phase Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA was successfully fabricated and subjected to comprehensive quasi-static and dynamic loading experiments to evaluate its energy release capability and mechanical properties for potential structural applications. The Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA demonstrated exceptional quasi-static mechanical performance, with a yield strength of 1490 MPa, an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa, and a fracture strain of 30%. Under dynamic loading at a strain rate of 3000 s−1, the alloy exhibited an even higher ultimate strength of 2300 MPa and maintained a fracture strain of 24%, showcasing its remarkable ability to retain plasticity under extreme conditions. Additionally, the Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA displayed significant chemical energy release and a high energy release capacity.
